designGate.prompt: Before writing code, sketch how one exchange's book will find its own best bid/ask quickly, and how the aggregator will turn N exchanges' BBOs into a single NBBO without rescanning every exchange's full book on every call. Name the per-exchange price-level container, the per-exchange best-price structure, and the index cancel will need later to update the NBBO without re-deriving it from scratch.

parts.title: Per-exchange BBO and the aggregate NBBO

hints.text: get_exchange_bbo and get_nbbo both boil down to 'find the best price on a side' — what do you need to answer that quickly as orders keep arriving?
A dict from price to the orders resting there gets you a level; a heap per side gets you the current best price without scanning every level each time you're asked.

Two dicts per exchange (price -> resting orders) plus a min-heap of ask prices and a max-heap of bid prices (negate for max) — the same shape as a single order book, minus any matching. get_nbbo() just asks every exchange for its own best_bid/best_ask and takes the max/min across whichever aren't None.

probes: What happens to your NBBO answer if two exchanges are quoting the exact same bid price?
Why does get_exchange_bbo need to handle an exchange_id it has never seen before?

parts.title: Size at the BBO, per exchange and aggregate

hints.text: Best price alone doesn't give you size — what do you already have that tells you everything resting at that price?
Once you know the best price at a level, its size is just summing qty over what's resting there. For the NBBO's size, which exchanges are even eligible to contribute?

get_exchange_bbo_size just sums the level dict at that exchange's own best price. get_nbbo_size has to filter first: only exchanges whose own best price equals the NBBO price contribute at all, then sum across just those — which can be more than one exchange when they tie.

probes: Why can't get_nbbo_size just take whichever exchange has the biggest size at its own best price?
What happens to get_nbbo_size if you add a huge order at a worse price than the NBBO?

parts.title: Cancel and its cross-exchange consequences

hints.text: cancel needs to go straight from an order id to where it's resting — same problem as cancel in any single order book.
Once cancel updates one exchange's own book, ask yourself: does that exchange's change ever ripple out into the NBBO, and when does it not?

Keep order_id -> exchange_id globally, and order_id -> (side, price) per exchange, both O(1) to maintain and update. After removing the order, recompute that one exchange's best_bid/best_ask (cheap — you already have the heap). get_nbbo() only actually changes if that exchange was the one supplying the NBBO price in the first place; otherwise recomputing it is a no-op.

probes: Cancel/replace an order by id — what data structure is doing the actual work, and why do heaps alone get painful once orders can leave the book?
Why does an efficient cancel matter more here than it would in a single exchange's book?

criteria: NBBO and per-exchange BBO exact after every add and cancel
NBBO derived by composition over per-exchange BBOs, not a second independent book
cancel updates the NBBO only when the cancelling exchange was setting it
heap for per-exchange best-price lookup, dict for O(1) id-based cancel
no full re-scan of an exchange's book on every get_nbbo call
tie-at-the-NBBO and cross-exchange edge cases considered before being told
stated when a cancel does and doesn't move the NBBO, and why
